dataset.what_one_row_represents: One holder of the office of UK Prime Minister (Wikidata Q14211, real humans only), with their Wikidata ID, first term start, Oxford/Cambridge flags, an overall classification, and the institutions they studied at.
dataset.time_range: 1721 (Robert Walpole) to 2024 (Keir Starmer); one undated holder

ana_01.label: The mirror image — Oxford makes PMs, Cambridge makes Nobels
ana_01.content: The two universities split Britain's elite almost perfectly down the middle. Oxford has educated 31 UK Prime Ministers to Cambridge's 15 — a 2.07-to-1 lead in politics. But flip to science and the ratio inverts: Cambridge claims 79 Nobel laureates to Oxford's 30, a 2.63-to-1 lead. Each university dominates exactly one domain and trails badly in the other. This is the headline of the whole dataset: the same two institutions that sit a few hours apart by train have spent three centuries quietly sorting the country's most ambitious people into rulers and discoverers.

calculation.output:
Oxford: PMs=31 Nobel=30 alumni=39259
Cambridge: PMs=15 Nobel=79 alumni=31284
PM ratio Oxford:Cambridge = 2.07:1
Nobel ratio Cambridge:Oxford = 2.63:1

data_table.description: Oxford vs Cambridge across the two prestige categories

ana_02.label: Where all 59 Prime Ministers were educated
ana_02.content: Of the 59 people who have held the office, 31 attended Oxford (including one — Henry Pelham — who attended both Oxford and Cambridge) and 15 attended Cambridge. Counting the dual-attendee once, that leaves 14 Cambridge-only PMs. Ten went to a university that was neither Oxford nor Cambridge, and four have no university recorded on Wikidata. Put another way, Oxbridge alone accounts for 76.3% of every Prime Minister Britain has ever had. The non-Oxbridge routes to Downing Street are the exception, not the rule.

calculation.output:
Total PMs: 59
Oxford (total incl both): 31  | Oxford only: 30
Cambridge (total incl both): 15 | Cambridge only: 14
Both: 1
Other university: 10
No university recorded: 4
Oxbridge share of all PMs: 76.3%

data_table.description: Education breakdown of all 59 UK Prime Ministers

ana_03.label: The regime change — Cambridge's silence since 1937
ana_03.content: The dataset's term-start dates expose a clean historical hinge. In the eighteenth century the two universities traded the premiership roughly evenly. But the last Cambridge-linked Prime Minister to take office was Stanley Baldwin in 1923; since then, Cambridge has produced nothing. Run the count forward from 1937 and the asymmetry is total: 14 Prime Ministers since then attended Oxford, and exactly zero attended Cambridge. Every PM who went to an English university in the last ninety years went to the same one.

calculation.output:
Last Cambridge-linked PM first term: 1923
First Oxford PM first term: 1742  Last: 2024
Since 1937, PMs whose university is Oxford-linked: 14
Since 1937, PMs whose university is Cambridge-linked: 0

data_table.description: PMs by university group across 20-year buckets of first-term year

ana_04.label: Christ Church — the college that made 13 Prime Ministers
ana_04.content: Oxford's dominance narrows to a single building. Thirteen Prime Ministers studied at Christ Church, more than any other college at either university — and more than most entire universities on earth. No other Oxford college comes close: Balliol is next with four, then Trinity with three. The route to Downing Street did not just run through Oxford; for much of British history it ran through one Oxford college.

calculation.output:
PMs whose record includes 'Christ Church': 13
Oxford college (first match) counts among Oxford PMs:
  Christ Church: 13
  Balliol College: 4
  Trinity College: 3
  Brasenose College: 2

data_table.description: Oxford colleges by number of PMs educated there (dataset)

ana_05.label: The Eton funnel
ana_05.content: Below the university is a school. Twenty of the 59 Prime Ministers were educated at Eton College — a single fee-paying school responsible for roughly a third of every PM in British history. Nine of them followed the exact same path: Eton, then Christ Church, Oxford. The narrowest, most-trodden route to power in Britain is one school feeding one college.

calculation.output:
PMs educated at Eton College (in dataset): 20
PMs educated at BOTH Eton and Christ Church (in dataset): 9

data_table.description: Eton / Christ Church pipeline among 59 PMs

ana_06.label: The Prime Ministers who broke the mould
ana_06.content: The pipeline has leaks worth naming. Four PMs have no university recorded: the 4th Duke of Devonshire, the genuinely non-graduate David Lloyd George and James Callaghan, and the undated Earl of Denbigh. Ten more took a route outside Oxbridge entirely — among them Winston Churchill, who went to Sandhurst not university; John Major, the most recent PM never to hold a degree; Benjamin Disraeli; the Duke of Wellington; Bonar Law and Gordon Brown, who took his PhD at Edinburgh and is the only post-1937 PM to attend an English-speaking university other than Oxford. These eleven names are the entire counterweight to three centuries of Oxbridge supremacy.

calculation.output:
No university recorded (4): ['William Cavendish, 4th Duke of Devonshire', 'David Lloyd George', 'James Callaghan', 'Basil Feilding, 6th Earl of Denbigh']
Other university (10): ['John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute', 'Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington', 'John Russell, 1st Earl Russell', 'Benjamin Disraeli', 'Bonar Law', 'Ramsay MacDonald', 'Neville Chamberlain', 'Winston Churchill', 'John Major', 'Gordon Brown']

ana_07.label: Normalising for notability — what the raw totals hide
ana_07.content: The raw Wikidata alumni totals (39,259 for Oxford, 31,284 for Cambridge) are a coverage artefact, not enrolment — they count only people famous enough to have a Wikidata entry, so they must never be read as 'Oxford is bigger'. But used carefully as a notability denominator they sharpen the story rather than confuse it. Per 1,000 recorded alumni, Oxford produces 0.79 Prime Ministers to Cambridge's 0.48 — a 1.65x political edge. For Nobels the gap is far larger: Cambridge yields 2.53 laureates per 1,000 recorded alumni to Oxford's 0.76, a 3.30x scientific edge. Even after correcting for who gets recorded, each university's specialism holds.

calculation.output:
Oxford PMs per 1,000 recorded alumni: 0.790
Cambridge PMs per 1,000 recorded alumni: 0.479
Oxford Nobels per 1,000 recorded alumni: 0.764
Cambridge Nobels per 1,000 recorded alumni: 2.525
Oxford PM-rate advantage over Cambridge: 1.65x
Cambridge Nobel-rate advantage over Oxford: 3.30x

data_table.description: Prestige rate per 1,000 recorded Wikidata alumni

ana_09.label: The full bench — all 59 PMs with portrait, term and college
ana_09.content: Every one of the 59 Prime Ministers can be matched to a real, attributed Wikimedia portrait via Wikidata QID, alongside their first term year, university group and college. Sorted chronologically, the deck runs from Robert Walpole (Cambridge, King's College, 1721) to Keir Starmer (Oxford, St Edmund Hall, 2024). The group tallies across the bench are Oxford 30, Cambridge 14, Both 1, Other 10, and None 4. This table powers the portrait gallery and the timeline, and is the visual spine of the piece.

data_table.description: All 59 PMs: name, term_start year, university group, college, portrait file, artist, license

ana_10.label: University head-to-head asset map (crests, logos, campus)
ana_10.content: The two universities are represented in the dataset's image cache by their official coat-of-arms, logo and a campus photograph each, sourced and attributed from Wikimedia Commons. Oxford (Q34433) supplies a public-domain coat of arms and logo plus an aerial campus panorama by Chensiyuan (CC BY-SA 4.0); Cambridge (Q35794) supplies a CC BY-SA 3.0 coat of arms and a St John's College courtyard photo by Diliff (CC BY-SA 3.0). These anchor the head-to-head comparison block visually.

caveats.content: 'Total alumni on Wikidata' (Oxford 39,259, Cambridge 31,284) is coverage-biased — it counts only people notable enough to have a Wikidata item with an educated-at field, never enrolment. Treat as relative notability coverage, not headcount.

Nobel counts use 'educated at', so a laureate can be linked as a former student OR as a later academic affiliate. Describe as 'associated with', not 'graduated from'. The dataset's 30/79 differs from PR figures (~76/121) because those use a broader 'affiliated with' definition.
The PM total of 59 includes pre-1801 Great Britain prime ministers and one undated holder (Earl of Denbigh), so it can differ by one or two from lists that start at a different date.

College attribution takes the first college matching a known Oxford/Cambridge college list; a few PMs attended more than one. Christ Church=13, Eton=20 are robust and match external sources (Oxford Summer Courses).
